how-much-to-charge-to-install-gutter-gua.text:
← Gutter guard bid calculator

How much to charge to install gutter guards

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$8/foot leaf filter special.” That number is not a takeoff. A one-story ranch with 140 feet of empty 5" K-style is not the same job as a two-story colonial with 220 feet of micromesh, twelve miters, packed leaves, and rotten fascia. The word “gutter guard” is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the feet and the stories, not just the special

Gutter-cleaning calculators price a seasonal debris flush and a downspout snake. Roofing calculators price squares, pitch, and a reroof. A gutter-guard install is a lineal-foot takeoff: the included ranch run, the extra story the coupon never mentions, the extra feet of coil, and the system. Quoting all of that from a published special is how the first extra story eats the field margin.

A job with a similar first-story gutter can cost much more

Each extra story is a taller ladder, a second-floor run, and time that never appears on the coupon. Extra feet over the included 120-foot ranch are billed as their own hours and extra coil. Packed gutters, extra miters, extra downspouts, fascia repair, steep-roof access, and occupied landscaping are adders that get forgotten on a screen special. On the sample rates a 2-story 220 ft micromesh colonial with a clean-first pass, two extra downspouts, 16 ft of fascia, and occupied access prices about $4,602 ($20.92 per foot, 15.3 crew-hours). The same shop’s 140 ft one-story screen ranch prices about $787 ($5.62 per foot, 2.7 hours, walk-away $566). Matching an $8/ft Facebook special on the colonial ($1,760) is how that job becomes a loss of about $1,553.

A reverse-curve steep roof is not automatically the expensive one

A 2-story 180 ft reverse-curve / helmet job with steep-roof access and occupied landscaping is not the micromesh colonial plus 20%. On the sample rates that reverse-curve job prices about $2,526 ($14.03 per foot, 7.7 crew-hours) — more as a total than the ranch, less than the packed micromesh, because the steep-roof hours do not live in a published per-foot adder. A typical 1-story 160 ft foam insert with two extra miters and occupied access prices about $1,296 (4.2 hours, $8.10 per foot). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine on the ranch turns into a loss after the first extra story.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $36/h installer loaded at 32% payroll burden is $47.52. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. On the sample rates the brochure ranch walk-away is $566, so an $8/ft coupon ($1,120) still covers that house. The same coupon on the colonial does not. Replace every rate with your coil and mesh invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a roofing inspection, a building-code determination, a leak warranty, a guarantee that any gutter will stay clear, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. System type, lineal feet, stories, miter count, and whether the gutters must be cleaned first are yours to confirm.

Price your next job

Common questions

How much to charge to install gutter guards?

Charge from the included one-story ranch, extra stories over that include, extra lineal feet over the included run, extra miters, extra downspouts, a clean-first pass on packed gutters, fascia repair, steep-roof access, occupied-home landscaping, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 1-story 140 ft screen ranch at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $787 — about $5.62 per foot.

Why is a flat $8/foot leaf-filter special dangerous?

Homeowners count 'a gutter is a gutter.' Extra stories, extra feet, extra miters, packed debris, rotten fascia, and a micromesh coil do not live in an $8/ft coupon. The special can look fine on a ranch and still lose more than $1,500 on a two-story colonial.

Does a longer gutter run always cost more per foot?

Not in proportion. On the sample rates a 2-story 220 ft micromesh colonial with a clean-first pass and fascia repair prices around $4,602 ($20.92 per foot), while a 140 ft one-story screen ranch prices around $787 ($5.62 per foot).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not construction, roofing, building-code, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why can a competitor advertise “$8 a foot installed”?

      Because that number is written around one specific house, and that house is the first preset here: a one-story ranch with 140 lineal feet of empty 5″ K-style, four miters, no extra downspouts, nobody home to work around. Priced honestly it really is cheap. What a per-foot special cannot see is the second story, the miter count, the downspouts, a clean-first pass, rotten fascia, and which guard is actually going on. Price your real house beside the special and the gap stops being an argument about who is honest and becomes a list of line items you can show the homeowner.

      What actually changes between screen, foam, reverse-curve, and micromesh?

      The setup time and the coil, and they move together. Perforated screen — the “$8-a-foot special” system — starts at 1.5 hours of base setup and $2.25 a foot of material. Foam inserts start at 1.7 hours and $3.40. Reverse-curve or helmet is 2.1 hours and $6.25 because it is fitted under the shingle course. Micromesh or leaf-filter is 2.4 hours and $8.50, which is most of why a mesh quote lands at three or four times a screen quote on the identical gutter run. Changing the system refills those two starting numbers and leaves every rate you have already typed alone.

      Why does a second story cost more than the same footage on a ranch?

      Because height is not footage, and the calculator bills them separately. Every extra 10 feet past the 120 included in a base setup adds 0.35 hours. A whole extra story adds 1.2 hours on its own, before a single extra foot is counted, and a steep roof adds another 0.9. That is ladder setting, walking the plank, and working off a roof edge instead of off a step ladder — the part a per-foot price silently averages away, and the reason a 180-foot colonial is not just “180 times the ranch rate.”

      Why are miters and downspouts priced separately from the run?

      Because a base setup already includes some of each — 120 feet, one story, four miters, and three downspouts by default — and only what is beyond that is billed. Each extra miter adds 0.15 hours plus an $8 kit; each extra downspout adds 0.25 hours plus a $22 adapter. A house with twelve corners is a different job from a rectangle with four, and this is where that shows up instead of quietly eating the margin.

      Should I clean the gutters before fitting, and what does it add?

      If they are full, fitting over the debris is how a guard job comes back as a callback. Ticking clean-first bills it: 0.2 hours per 10 feet across the whole run, plus a $35 disposal cost. On the 220-foot mesh preset that is 4.4 hours of crew time — real money that a homeowner comparing your bid to a coupon price will not have in theirs, which is exactly why it belongs on the proposal as its own line rather than folded into a rate.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, and a bid link you copy carries those same numbers in the page’s address rather than sending anything to a server. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your footage, wages, or prices.

      What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

      The bid price already carries your target margin on top of labor, coil, kits, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — crew hours, guard material, miter kits, downspout adapters, fascia, disposal, travel and equipment — the point below which the install stops being profitable at all. Typing a number into “Price you’re considering” shows you the margin, or the loss, before you send it.

vs-a-flat-8-per-foot-special.html.text:
← Gutter Guard Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $8/ft leaf-filter special

Gutter-guard shops are shopped against a flat $8-a-foot leaf-filter special. That rate cannot see the job — stories, miters, extra downspouts, a clean-first pass through packed gutters, and fascia repair decide whether the footage pays, and two runs of the same length can differ by thousands of dollars in real cost.

What a flat $8/ft special is

A price per foot is the fastest number to advertise on a postcard or a coupon page: measure the run, multiply by a rate, read back a total. It is also the unit homeowners already bring with them when they call for a quote.

The rate was priced from a specific job — typically a one-story ranch with a clean, empty run and a handful of corners — and then reused for the next lineal-foot number that calls in, whether or not that next job shares any of those.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter lineal feet of gutter, stories, miters, extra downspouts, system type — screen, foam, reverse-curve, or micromesh — whether the gutters need a clean-first pass, fascia repair feet, occupied-home access, and steep-roof access, plus your own wage, payroll burden, travel and equipment, overhead, and target margin. It prices access hours, miters, downspouts, clean-first, and fascia separately — for this job, not a rate carried over from the last one.

What a flat $8/ft rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $8/ft for a one-story ranch with empty gutters and a two-story colonial with packed gutters and rotten fascia, even though stories and prep are where the extra hours live. Prices extra stories, a clean-first pass, and fascia repair as their own line items, so a harder job costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for miters or extra downspouts — a run of four corners and a run of twelve get the same rate. Prices miters and downspouts above the included count as their own hours and hardware.
Has no line for system type — a $2.25/ft screen coil and an $8.50/ft micromesh coil get quoted the same. Prices coil or mesh material per foot by system type: screen, foam, reverse-curve, or micromesh.
Bundles clean-first and fascia repair inside the same blended per-foot number, if the crew notices them at all before quoting. Nets clean-first hours and fascia repair hours and material out as their own lines, priced only when the job needs them.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price per foot and the walk-away price alongside the total, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

Same $8/ft rate, two different jobs

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs — $36 hourly wage, 32% burden, $45 travel and equipment, 16% overhead, 28% target margin, 120 ft / 1 story / 4 miters / 3 downspouts included:

A 140 ft one-story ranch with empty gutters, 4 miters, no extra downspouts, and no fascia repair — close to the job an $8/ft special is shopped from — takes 2.7 crew-hours and prices at $786.71 for the job — $5.62 a foot, already under the flat special.

Bid a 220 ft two-story colonial instead — micromesh, 12 miters, 2 extra downspouts, a clean-first pass through packed gutters, and 16 ft of fascia repair — and it takes 15.3 crew-hours, costs $3,313.08 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $4,601.50 — $20.92 a foot. Quoting that job at the flat $8/ft special reproduces $1,760.00 for 220 feet, which is $1,553.08 below the job's own break-even cost — before counting the $2,841.50 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 28% target margin. Same advertised rate, one job that pays and one that loses money before the truck leaves.

Common questions

Why does a flat $8/ft leaf-filter special get a gutter-guard bid wrong?

Because lineal feet alone does not measure the job. A 140 ft one-story ranch with empty gutters -- close to the job the $8/ft special is shopped from -- takes about 2.7 crew-hours and this calculator prices it at $786.71, or $5.62 a foot, already under the flat special. The same $8/ft rate applied to a 220 ft two-story colonial with 12 miters, 2 extra downspouts, a clean-first pass through packed gutters, and 16 ft of fascia repair reproduces a $1,760.00 quote, on a job this calculator prices at $4,601.50 and that costs $3,313.08 to run before a dollar of profit -- so the flat rate does not just thin the margin, it quotes $1,553.08 under break-even.

What does a flat per-foot rate usually miss entirely?

Stories, miters, extra downspouts, whether the gutters need to be cleaned out before the guard goes on, and fascia condition. A flat rate has no line for a second story's ladder and staging time, no line for eight extra miters over the four a ranch run already includes, no line for two extra downspouts, no line for clearing a fall's worth of packed leaves first, and no line for rotten fascia that has to be replaced before anything can be hung.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs: a 140 ft one-story ranch with empty gutters, 4 miters, no extra downspouts, and no fascia repair takes 2.7 crew-hours and prices at $786.71 -- $5.62 a foot, already under the $8 special. A 220 ft two-story colonial with 12 miters, 2 extra downspouts, a clean-first pass through packed gutters, and 16 ft of fascia repair takes 15.3 crew-hours, costs $3,313.08 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $4,601.50 -- $20.92 a foot. Quoting that job at the flat $8/ft special reproduces $1,760.00 for 220 feet, which is $1,553.08 below the job's own break-even cost -- before counting the $2,841.50 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 28% target margin.

Is a flat per-foot rate ever a reasonable shorthand?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- one story, a handful of miters, empty gutters, sound fascia, the same system the rate was learned on -- a per-foot number can land close. The risk is quoting a two-story job, a packed clean-first, or rotten fascia the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know the stories, the miters, or the fascia condition until the crew is on the roof, and by then the per-foot number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your supplier's coil and mesh pricing. It takes lineal feet, stories, miters, extra downspouts, system type, a clean-first pass, fascia repair, occupancy, and roof pitch, plus your own wage, payroll burden, travel and equipment, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into install hours and a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-foot rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Gutter Guard Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read how much to charge to install gutter guards.

Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, and supply costs, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or submitting a bid. This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is an account-based platform for running a home service company's whole operation, including scheduling the crew and invoicing the customer once a job is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this gutter-guard job cost, given its feet, stories, and extras, before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

Jobber is a field service management platform used by home service businesses — lawn care, cleaning, HVAC, plumbing, gutter and other exterior trades among them — to run client management and online quoting, scheduling and crew dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client-facing hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Jobber's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of field service software describe scheduling, invoicing and collecting payment for a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a gutter-guard install should cost from lineal feet, stories, miters, and system type before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage a client list, dispatch a crew across a season, or collect a payment. It takes one gutter-guard job's lineal feet, stories, miters, extra downspouts, and system type — screen, foam, reverse-curve, or micromesh — with a clean-first pass, fascia repair, steep-roof access, and occupied-home landscaping as their own line items, plus loaded installer wage, payroll burden, travel and equipment, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price, the price per foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job.
